newsitem.title: ANGOLA: Angola asks neighbours to restrict UNITA flights.
newsitem.headline: Angola asks neighbours to restrict UNITA flights.

text.p: Angola has asked Botswana, Namibia and South Africa to restrict flights into territory held by the opposition UNITA movement, diplomats and officials said on Tuesday.
"The Angolan government is talking to the South Africans, the Namibians and Botswana about stopping flights into UNITA areas," one Western diplomat told Reuters.
South African embassy officials in Luanda said they were not aware of any Angolan request to South Africa to restrict flights to UNITA zones.
Diplomats and officials close to the peace process have said in recent weeks that the country was drifting toward war as the government and UNITA positioned troops and arms around the country.
UNITA (National Union for the Total Independence of Angola) and the government fought a two-decade civil war that ended when the sides signed a peace treaty in 1994.
Although the former rebels entered a power-sharing agreement with the government in April, UNITA still controls vast areas of the countryside.
Last month UNITA agreed to a series of U.N. Security Council proposals including handing over its territory to the government and defining the number of troops it still has under arms.
But diplomats and officials say the former rebels have shown little inclination to go along with the proposals.
Fuel and arms sanctions are in place against UNITA and the Security Council has threatened sanctions on travel and banking if UNITA does not comply.

Most UNITA supplies came from the former Zaire before the fall of veteran president Mobutu Sese Seko to Laurent Kabila in May. Now most flights to UNITA areas come from South Africa, diplomats, military officials and pilots say.
"Most of the cargo flights into Bailundo, Andulo and Lusamba are coming from South Africa these days," one contract pilot told Reuters, referring to three important UNITA cities in the interior.
Officials close to the peace process say the government has indicated in recent days its willingness to give the new sanctions a chance before embarking on a military offensive against UNITA.
"They have said they are going to wait and give the sanctions a chance," said the official.
"But they aren't going to wait forever, especially if the sanctions are not working. This effort to shut down the flights is meant to squeeze them even more," the official said.
